schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch mark the harsh 'quousque tandem' opening; 'these things' means 'of such kind,' Job's words like the wind in emptiness and a boisterous wind in vehemence, impugning the justice of the Absolute One.
Henry: Bildad reproves Job with a greater passion than Job's own; right that God perverts not judgment (Gen 18:25), but unfair in dragging in the children's death as proof of their sin.
Gill introduces Bildad the Shuhite, agreed beforehand with his fellows on their common side; the friends came like the messengers of Job's losses, one before another had done.
Clarke traces Bildad to Shuah, son of Abraham by Keturah, of the east country (Gen 25:2), and lays out the argument of the whole chapter.

themes: a true doctrine turned to a false charge

schools.summary: Clarke: 'charge God foolishly' — the affliction proves wrath, and wrath proves sin; he prefers the Arabic/Syriac 'spirit of pride.' Wesley: the strong wind is speech 'boisterous and violent.'
Gill hears wonder, anger, impatience, and contempt in 'how long wilt thou speak' — some render it 'how long wilt thou trifle after this manner?'
Keil and Delitzsch read a poetical 'mighty wind' (cf. 1:19) — Job's speeches like wind in their nothingness and a boisterous wind in their vehemence.
Henry: Job had pleaded his words were but wind (6:26); Bildad retorts they are a strong wind, to be fenced against rather than heard.

themes: the friend who will not listen

schools.summary: Wesley finds in the divine names (the Mighty, the Almighty, the All-sufficient) a proof that God, self-sufficient and un-tempted, cannot pervert judgment; Clarke turns the axiom on Job — 'can he afflict thee for naught?'
Gill: the doubled question emphatically denies any injustice in God, set against Job, whom Bildad supposes to have charged God with wrong toward him and his children.

themes: a sound premise, a cruel inference

schools.summary: Gill reports and half-endorses Bildad: the children 'no doubt' sinned notoriously and were righteously punished (Broughton: 'sent into the hand of their trespass'); the pliant particle may read if/seeing/because/though.
Clarke voices the inference: the children were cut off because by transgression they had filled the measure of iniquity; 'cast away' = sent to the place of their sin.
Ellicott renders literally 'then he sent them away' — by means of their own transgression it became their destruction.
Henry protests: extraordinary afflictions are not always the punishment of extraordinary sins but sometimes the trial of graces (Luke 13:2-4) — 'here Bildad missed it.'

debates.question: Does the manner of the children's death prove they were sinners above others?

sides.position: Yes — their destruction was the righteous wages of their sin
No — heavy affliction may be the trial of graces, not the punishment of guilt

schools.summary: Clarke: the sparing of Job (where his children fell) proves God 'waits to be gracious'; Wesley: 'betimes' = rise early to seek him, speedily and diligently.
Gill: seek God in the morning, first and above all, without procrastination and with the whole heart, for he rewards them that diligently seek him.
Henry: the same counsel Eliphaz gave (5:8); Bildad means to condemn while seeming to comfort, yet the advice is sound — the prayer of the upright prevails (Prov 15:8; Ps 66:18).
Keil and Delitzsch: 'to turn oneself to God earnestly seeking'; 'the habitation of thy righteousness' is the home God restores to a man pure in his inmost mind.

Ellicott: the 'if' yields but one inference — 'thou art not pure and upright,' the wounds of an unfaithful friend; he sets up the two characters and paints the wicked as the paper-reed that withers in abundance. Keil: the appeal to the fathers recalls Deut 32:7.
Clarke reads 'the habitation of thy righteousness' as strong irony — were thy house a temple of God, would it lie in ruins? Wesley takes it of Job's house and family managed with righteousness.
Gill: the 'if' tacitly denies Job's purity, though God called him perfect; he turns 'pure' toward the heart cleansed by faith in Christ's blood.

themes: if thou wert pure and upright

schools.summary: Gill: the 'small beginning' set against a greater latter end — Job was in fact given double (Broughton: 'thy former state should be little to thy latter').
Clarke: to reward a piety that had lost all things, God would multiply Job's former prosperity beyond anything he had possessed.
Henry: God enriches not per saltum but per gradum — dawning light to noonday, mustard seed to tree; despise not the day of small things (Zech 4:10).

Henry: Bildad owns 'we are of yesterday' and refers to the ancients nearer revelation; but now we have the written word (Rom 10:8; Ps 119:99) and need not inquire of the former age — nor will he go as far as Eliphaz (4:7).
Keil and Delitzsch hear an echo of Deut 32:7; 'the search of the fathers' is the collected wisdom of experience, our shadowy life no fit judge of God's dealings.
Gill: history shows good men delivered (Noah, Abraham, Lot) and the wicked perished (Cain's line, Babel, Sodom); 'former age,' not the 'first age' of the LXX.
Clarke takes 'the former age' of the first generation, the patriarchs, a remote antiquity; Wesley: search the ancient records seriously and industriously.

debates.question: How far back does 'the former age' reach?

sides.position: the generations gone before, not the first age of the world
the very first generation, the patriarchs — a remote antiquity

schools.summary: Clarke: the long-lived ancients had room to observe, while our days are a shadow — the sundial's 'Umbrae sumus' and David's 'our days are as a shadow' (1 Chron 29:15); Wesley: we are lately born, with little experience.
Gill: 'yesterday' means a short space, set against the antediluvian fathers of nine hundred years; the friends themselves were gray-headed and aged.
Keil and Delitzsch: the verse is the hinge for the papyrus figure — prosperity like a reed on ground that wants perpetual water.

themes: a shadow cannot judge the eternal

schools.summary: Clarke: treat the fathers' maxims with deference, the fruit of long experience; Wesley: they utter their words sincerely, from deep consideration, from their own knowledge, not hearsay.
Gill: the former age and their fathers are Job's appointed teachers, from whom to expect instruction useful to his case.

themes: a good principle bent to overbear

schools.summary: Clarke: 'gome' is beyond doubt the Egyptian papyrus (LXX 'papyros'), needing the Nile's water; the flag the ropemakers' reed. Wesley: the hypocrite's hope needs false ground as the rush needs mire.
Gill: the 'rush' the bulrush, named in Hebrew from its drinking of water, delighting in moist and marshy clay.
Ellicott: the 'flag' is the plant of Gen 41:2 that the cattle fed on, and the figure is reinforced by the spider's web, the most fragile of tenements.

sides.position: the Egyptian papyrus / paper-reed of the Nile
the bulrush that grows in marshy clay

themes: can the rush grow without mire

schools.summary: Clarke: a short-lived succulent, 'soon ripe, soon rotten'; Wesley: its greenness promises long continuance, yet it withers of itself, sooner than the hardier herbs.
Gill: before ripeness, without moisture, it changes and fades, dying by no hand.
Keil and Delitzsch: the subject is never the reed but the ungodly likened to it, half figure and half literal.
Henry: green for show, light and hollow; the grass is cut down then withers (Ps 90:6), but the rush withers uncut (Ps 129:6).

themes: it withereth before any other herb

schools.summary: Gill: the forgetters of God — forgetting his being, works, benefits, and worship — are unfruitful as bulrush and flag, standing in the mire of the unregenerate state.
Clarke argues 'chaneph' means polluted/profligate, not 'hypocrite' (who could have no hope), while this man does have hope; Wesley: 'paths' = the events that befall them, God's manner of dealing.
Henry: forgetfulness of God lies at the bottom of hypocrisy and of the vain hopes with which men flatter themselves.

outliers.note: Argues 'hypocrite' mistranslates chaneph, which means polluted/defiled; a true hypocrite could have no hope, but this man does, so the word names the profligate, not the pretender.

themes: the paths of all that forget God

schools.summary: Clarke: hoping on till the last thread of life is cut, with no more strength than a spider's web (Good: 'their support rot away'); Wesley: the 'hope' is the man's wealth and glory, cut off suddenly, the web easily swept down.
Gill: the doom repeated for certainty; the Hebrew carries loathing — 'whom his hope shall loathe,' the man vexing himself for so vain a trust.
Henry: the hope is woven from the man's own bowels, as the spider (not the bee) spins from itself, and is swept away when God purges his house.

themes: whose trust shall be a spider's web
a thread that will not bear his weight

schools.summary: Clarke's close observation: the spider tests and repairs its web, retires secure, and is swept away by the besom in a moment; Wesley: the 'house' is children, servants, and wealth, that refuge of lies swept away.
Gill: the house is the ground of confidence — riches or works of righteousness; to lean on it is to make flesh one's arm and build upon the sand.
Ellicott marks that 'the description of the wicked man ends here.'
Henry: the formal professor leans on his web and takes hold as the spider in kings' palaces (Prov 30:28), only to have it fail when he most needs it.

themes: he shall lean upon his house

schools.summary: Gill: a tall, vigorous tree — the hypocrite in his prosperity, green in leaves but a profession without fruit.
Clarke: a luxuriant plant struck by a sudden blast, dying from the root; Wesley: a well-rooted tree, green and public, his branches his children, yet suddenly cut off.
Henry: the green bay-tree (Ps 37:35) and Nebuchadnezzar's tree (Dan 4:10), given every advantage and yet cut off.

Keil and Delitzsch keep the ungodly as the subject throughout; Ellicott dissents, reading an opposite picture marked by the emphatic pronoun — the genuinely verdant, contrasted with the paper-reed (cf. v.6).

debates.question: Is the flourishing 'green' tree of vv.16-19 the wicked man, or an opposite figure?

sides.position: the hypocrite / wicked, given every advantage yet suddenly destroyed
an opposite picture — the genuinely flourishing, set over against the withering reed

themes: he is green before the sun

schools.summary: Ellicott: the roots draw moisture from a perennial fountain, and 'the place of stones' is rather 'the house of stones,' the durable stone edifice; even plucked up, the tree leaves offshoots. Keil: the close sounds like the Psalms — God ready to 'take by the hand' (Isa 41:13).
Gill: the roots wrapped about the heap picture the seeming stability of the hypocrite, like the seed sown on stony ground.
Wesley: the stony heap signifies firmness — roots embracing the stones in solid, not sandy, ground.

themes: his roots wrapped about the heap

schools.summary: Gill: the sun's heat, or an uprooting, or God removing the hypocrite from the garden (the church), from esteem among men, or from the world as a cumberer of the ground.
Clarke: a reference to the loss of an inheritance, the very ground saying 'I know thee not'; Wesley: God the destroyer, the man so extirpated that no memorial is left.
Henry: rooted out so entirely that the place says 'I have not seen thee' (Ps 37:36), neither root nor branch left him (Mal 4:1).

themes: if he destroy him from his place

schools.summary: Clarke reads strong irony: the scape-grace levelled, another growing from his soil; he rejects Good's turn of the verse upon God, comparing the sardonic 'rejoice, O young man' (Eccl 11:9). Wesley: all his joy comes to this, another tree grows in his place.
Gill: the 'joy of his way' is the short exultation of prosperity, issuing in destruction from his place — 'behold' marking its strange certainty.
Henry: the way of the ungodly perishes (Ps 1:6); others fill his place, no more warned by his fall than he was by another's.

outliers.voice: John Mason Good (as reported by Clarke)
outliers.note: Renders the verse of God himself — 'behold the Eternal, exulting in his course; even over his dust shall raise up another' — a reading Clarke rejects as unsupported by the ancient versions and against the irony of the place.

themes: this is the joy of his way
the way of the ungodly perishes

schools.summary: Henry: Bildad reasons 'as he fared, so he was' — true that God casts not away the upright nor takes the ungodly by the hand (Luke 16:26), but the inference from Job's ruin to his guilt is neither just nor charitable.
Gill: 'a perfect man' is the upright, perfect not in himself but in Christ, by justification not sanctification; such a one God never casts away.
Clarke: another ancient maxim — God saves the righteous and roots out the wicked; Wesley: yet the good man may not be lifted up in this world, so Bildad's inference fails.
Keil and Delitzsch: 'help' is 'to take by the hand' of one owned as God's own (Isa 41:13); the close of the speech runs like a psalm.

themes: God will not cast away a perfect man
as he fared so he was

schools.summary: Clarke reads the close as a prayer, Bildad less virulent than Eliphaz, and the maxim contradicted by the afflicted patriarchs (Abel, Abram, Jacob, Joseph, Moses) — 'by their fruits ye shall know them' (Matt 7:16). Wesley: pure encouragement, God ceasing not to do good till he gives joy.
Gill: the promise addressed to Job if upright, joy as at a jubilee; yet a tacit charge that Job is an evil-doer, since outward adversity is no rule of God's love or hatred.
Ellicott: 'he will yet fill thy mouth with laughter' — Bildad's unsympathetic selfishness, suspecting a secret sin while holding out hope of restoration.

themes: a maxim contradicted by the patriarchs

schools.summary: Henry: the enemies clothed with shame when they see the saints honoured; the wicked's dwelling comes to nought, for only those who make God their dwelling are safe (Ps 90:1) — yet Bildad's inference against Job is unjust.
Gill: 'they that hate thee' are the Chaldeans and Sabeans who plundered Job, clothed with a shame as visible as the clothes on a man's back when they see him restored.
Wesley: God helps not the evil-doer, whose tent shall be no more, yet casts not away the good man though he be cast down for a season.
Keil and Delitzsch: the triumphant close, with its shamed enemies and vanished tent, sounds throughout like the language of the Psalms.

themes: the dwelling place come to nought
the God who is our dwelling
a psalm-like close, a quiet accusation
